bib.title: Large Language Models Are State-of-the-Art Evaluators of Translation Quality

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Large Language Models Are State-of-the-Art Evaluators of Translation Quality", Tom Kocmi and Christian Federmann (Microsoft). The extraction is arXiv 2302.14520v2, dated 31 May 2023. The EAMT 2023 venue does not appear anywhere in the extracted text, so it is unconfirmed from this PDF.
File: /Users/ramsey-wise/workspace/learn-ai-engineering/generative-ai/08-eval/sources/kocmi-2023-large-language-models-state-art.pdf

COVERAGE: Read all 39,974 of 39,974 chars, including Limitations, Tables 1–8 and Appendices A (prompts), B (full results) and C (Ada answers). I skimmed the references for where the method comes from.

AUDIT OF NOTE (generative-ai/08-eval/notes/05-llm-as-judge.md, ~line 63)
- 89.8% / COMET-22 83.9% / BLEU 70.8%: CORRECT. All three are in Table 2. The 89.8% is GEMBA-GPT4-DA in **reference-based** mode (prompt is DA, 0–100), measured as system-level pairwise accuracy on WMT22 MQM 2022 for en-de, en-ru and zh-en. The note does not say it is reference-based, and it should, because the 60.6% figure that follows is from the no-reference variant. "Ahead of every trained metric" is true. The strongest trained metric is MetricX XXL at 85.0%. The no-reference GPT4-DA scores 87.6%, which also beats every metric.
- τ 0.36–0.38 vs COMET-22 0.37–0.43: CORRECT against Table 4 (GPT4-DA: 0.36/0.36/0.38; COMET-22: 0.37/0.40/0.43 for en-de/en-ru/zh-en). The rule is Kendall tau-b. "Trailed" holds for the DA prompt only. GEMBA-GPT4-SQM[noref] scores 0.359/0.432/0.416 (Appendix B), which beats COMET-22 on en-ru (0.432 vs 0.400). So "per segment it trailed" should be pinned to GPT4-DA.
- 60.6% at 95: PARTLY CORRECT. Table 5 gives 60.6% for GPT-4 DA[noref], but the body text says "60.5%". The paper contradicts itself. The table is the source and the note's figure matches it. For reference-based DA (the 89.8% variant) the share at 95 is 53.3%.
- "per-item ties were everywhere and only the averages separated systems": OVERSTATED. The authors frame the tie explanation as a conjecture ("We conjecture that frequent segment-level ties ... may contribute"). The note states it as fact.
- "GEMBA shows what a wide numeric scale does": NOT SUPPORTED by this paper, and arguably the reverse. The paper's own contribution claim is that "the least constrained template achieves the best performance", and its Figure 1 caption calls the DA 0–100 prompt "best-performing". Narrower scales did not fix segment-level τ:
  - GPT4-Classes (5 labels, ref) gets τ 0.222/0.267/0.273, worse than DA's 0.357/0.358/0.382.
  - GPT4-Stars (1–5) gets 0.326/0.351/0.382.

  At system level, GPT-4 Stars and Classes[noref] reach 91.2%, above DA's 89.8%. The paper never tests the claim that wide scales hurt. The note uses GEMBA to illustrate the Huyen point, and that framing needs rewording.
- "Models below GPT-3.5 gave unusable output": CORRECT. GPT-2 and Ada gave no in-range replies, and Babbage and Curie were "close to random guessing".
- "3 language pairs, 54 systems, professional MQM labels, zero-shot": CORRECT.

CLAIMS

LIMITS
- Results cover only 3 high-resource language pairs. The authors expect performance to drop for under-resourced languages.
- SOTA holds at system level only ("GEMBA's state-of-the-art performance only holds for the system level"). The authors say "more analysis is needed before using it as the main tool".
- Training-data contamination cannot be ruled out. The authors argue it is unlikely because the test set was released Dec 2022, after OpenAI's Sep 2021 data cutoff.
- Zero-shot only, segment-by-segment, with no document context.
- Invalid answers are re-sampled at higher temperature, which adds some non-determinism.
- ChatGPT and part of GPT-4 are excluded from the failure counts.
- There are no significance tests or confidence intervals on the accuracies.
- Dated: the models are text-davinci-002/003, text-chat-davinci-002 and early gpt-4, all now retired.

BUILDS ON: WMT22 Metrics task (Freitag et al., 2022a/b); pairwise accuracy (Kocmi et al., 2021); MQM (Freitag et al., 2021a); DA/SQM templates from Appraise (Federmann, 2018); DA scale (Graham et al., 2013); Kendall tau variants (Callison-Burch et al., 2011; Macháček and Bojar, 2014); GPT translation (Hendy et al., 2023); related work by Lu et al. (2023).

CODE: GEMBA-DA prompt (Fig. 1 / App. A.1, p.3/p.10). The "human reference" line is dropped in noref mode.
```
Score the following translation from {source_lang} to {target_lang} with respect
to the human reference on a continuous scale from 0 to 100, where score of zero means
"no meaning preserved" and score of one hundred means "perfect meaning and grammar".
{source_lang} source: "{source_seg}"
{target_lang} human reference: {reference_seg}
{target_lang} translation: "{target_seg}"
Score:
```

FIGURES: Figure 1, p.3: "The best-performing prompt based on Direct Assessment expecting a score between 0–100." It is the only figure: the whole method is one prompt, which shows faster than prose how bare the judge is. Table 5 (p.4, the score histogram) explains the clumping better than words do.

PROBLEMS
- The paper contradicts itself in three places:
  - 60.5% (text) vs 60.6% (Table 5).
  - "least constrained template achieves the best performance" vs GPT-4 Stars and Classes[noref] at 91.2%, above DA's 89.8%.
  - Section 2.3 says "seven GPT models", but Table 1 and the abstract list nine.
- Section 4.4 has a garbled sentence: systems with more 95s are said to get "a lower average score".
- The extraction lost the bold formatting that marks the ref-only prompt lines and the bolded Table 3 cells.
- The text contains no embedded instructions.
